ch01.anchor: Selected Historical and Cultural Materials of Shanghai
ch01.note: The wenshi ziliao (‘cultural and historical materials’) series, part of a nationwide project begun in 1959 under the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference—the CPPCC, the People’s Republic’s united-front advisory body. Committees at every level gathered memoirs from surviving participants in pre-1949 life—former officials, officers, businessmen, and, as here, gang members—to preserve first-hand material. The genre is candid but shaped by its moment: written under an official frame, the volumes mix valuable eyewitness detail with the political vocabulary of their day.

ch01.anchor: The names Green Gang and Hong Gang
ch01.note: The two great secret-society brotherhoods of the Chinese underworld. The Green Gang (青帮, Qingbang), grown from the Grand Canal grain-transport guilds, dominated Shanghai. The Hong Gang (洪帮)—also the Hongmen (洪门), loosely the ‘Red Gang’—was the sworn-brotherhood network of south China descended from the anti-Qing Triads. As the note concedes, the writers here name them inconsistently, and this translation keeps each writer’s usage.

ch02.note: The standard frame of Chinese Marxist historiography for the century from the Opium War (1840) to 1949: China as ‘semi-colonial’ (dominated by foreign powers through treaty ports and concessions rather than formally colonized) and ‘semi-feudal’ (its landlord-peasant order eroded but not replaced). The preface reads the gangs through this lens throughout.

The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom (太平天国, 1851–64), the vast religious-political rebellion against the Qing led by Hong Xiuquan, which convulsed south and central China at a cost of tens of millions of lives.

The Small Sword Society (小刀会), a Triad-linked secret society, seized the walled Chinese city of Shanghai in September 1853 and held it seventeen months before the Qing retook it in February 1855. Overlapping the Taiping war, it is treated in official history as an early anti-feudal, anti-imperialist revolt.

ch02.anchor: the recovery of Shanghai in the Revolution of 1911
ch02.note: In the Revolution of 1911 (the Xinhai Revolution) that ended the Qing dynasty, gang and secret-society forces helped wrest Shanghai from the imperial authorities in November 1911. ‘Recovery’ (光复) is the period word for a city’s passing out of Qing hands.

The purge of 12 April 1927, when Chiang Kai-shek turned on his Communist allies in Shanghai. Green Gang gunmen—marshalled with Du Yuesheng, Huang Jinrong, and Zhang Xiaolin—fell on the Communist-led pickets and unions at dawn, and thousands died in the terror that followed. It is the hinge of this whole book: the moment the Shanghai gangs became instruments of the Nationalist state. Corroborated by all standard accounts.

The Cultural Revolution (1966–76), by its official PRC name (十年浩劫). Writing in 1986, the preface makes the era’s conventional move of tracing the gangs’ lingering ‘poison’ to Lin Biao (Mao’s designated heir, who died in 1971 fleeing an alleged coup) and the ‘Gang of Four’ (Jiang Qing and her allies, blamed after 1976 for the upheaval)—a rhetorical link, not a documented one.

ch03.note: 1905–1996; the author. A postal clerk who rose through both the Green Gang and the Nationalist labour machine to chair the Shanghai General Labour Union, he broke with the Kuomintang in 1948, joined the new regime, and became a government minister and vice-chairman of the NPC Standing Committee—the official who also brushed this book’s title. His memoir is thus an insider’s account, written from within the establishment it describes.
1899–1967; a founding labour organizer of the Chinese Communist Party, a leader of the May Thirtieth Movement, and, in 1930, briefly its paramount leader (the ‘Li Lisan line’).

ch03.anchor: the Rihua Cotton Mill in Pudong
ch03.note: The Rihua (Nihua) mill (日华纱厂), a Sino-Japanese cotton mill across the Huangpu in Pudong, was an early battleground of the Shanghai labour movement; the author cites its lost strike as a lesson in the gangs’ power.
1898–1927; pioneer Communist labour organizer in Shanghai, active among the Pudong mill and dock workers; executed by the Nationalists in 1927.

Anyuan, a colliery and rail town on the Hunan–Jiangxi border, was the site of a celebrated Communist-led miners’ and railwaymen’s movement in the early 1920s (Li Lisan and Liu Shaoqi among its organizers), in which the Party learned to work with—and through—the local secret societies.

The nationwide anti-imperialist upsurge touched off on 30 May 1925, when British-officered police in the Shanghai International Settlement shot dead demonstrators protesting the killing of a Chinese worker at a Japanese mill. It set off strikes and boycotts across China and was a turning point for the labour and revolutionary movements.

A secure, lifelong livelihood; the metal bowl will not break as an earthenware one would. The author’s ranking—a customs post a ‘golden’ bowl, a bank post ‘silver,’ the post office ‘iron’—grades the era’s coveted salaried jobs by how secure each was thought to be.

‘Yellow’ unions (黄色工会), in the labour-movement vocabulary of the day, were the state- and employer-tolerated unions—here the Kuomintang-controlled bodies—as opposed to the Communist-led ‘red’ unions driven underground after 1927.

Entering a gang boss’s ‘door’ as a disciple (门生) meant a formal master-pupil bond, sealed by presenting a written pledge; it created lifelong obligations of protection upward and loyalty downward. The author, an educated union official, took Du Yuesheng as master purely for the leverage the tie conferred—a candour characteristic of this memoir.

ch03.anchor: constant as the moon in its fullness
ch03.note: The Heng Society’s name puns on Du Yuesheng: heng (恒, ‘constant’) evokes the phrase ‘constant as the moon at the full,’ while yue (月, ‘moon’) is the middle graph of Du’s given name Yuesheng. The society’s emblem—a bell (a homophone of sheng) beneath a new moon—spells the name a second way.

The ‘January Twenty-Eighth Incident’ of 1932: Japanese forces attacked the Zhabei district of Shanghai on 28 January and fought the Chinese 19th Route Army for weeks before a truce. It devastated the city’s northern industrial quarter and deepened the slump the author describes.

ch03.anchor: the December Ninth student movement in Beiping
ch03.note: The student demonstrations that began in Beiping (Beijing) on 9 December 1935, demanding resistance to Japanese encroachment in north China; they helped touch off the national salvation movement of 1935–37.
‘White’ Russians—émigrés who had fled the Bolshevik revolution—formed a large, often destitute community in Shanghai and were a ready pool of strike-breakers and armed guards for foreign firms.

Funatsu Tatsuichirō (1873–1947), a Japanese diplomat and, in the 1930s, chairman of the association of Japanese cotton mills in China; his appeal to Du Yuesheng to mediate the 1936 general strike measures the gang boss’s standing with foreign capital.

Chiang’s statement at the Lushan hill resort in mid-July 1937, after the Marco Polo Bridge clash, declaring that China would fight if pushed to ‘the last extremity’—widely taken as the Nationalist government’s commitment to full resistance against Japan.

During the Battle of Shanghai (August–November 1937), Du Yuesheng and Dai Li’s secret service armed irregular units (别动队) drawn largely from Green Gang and Hongmen men and from workers; the author commanded one of the five detachments. Poorly armed and barely used, they were disbanded when the city fell.
Xiang Songpo, better known as Xiang Haiqian (1888–1974): a leader of the Hongmen’s ‘Five Lakes’ lodges and a 1911 revolutionary, who used the brotherhoods for anti-Japanese organizing in this period.

Lu Liankui, former chief detective inspector of the International Settlement police, and Lu Bohong (Joseph Lo Pa Hong), a prominent Catholic industrialist who headed a Japanese-sponsored ‘maintenance’ body—both assassinated as collaborators early in the occupation. The author’s claim that his hidden pistols were the weapons used is his own; the killings themselves are attested.

ch03.anchor: After Shanghai became a solitary island
ch03.note: The ‘solitary island’ (孤岛) period: after the Chinese city fell in November 1937, the foreign concessions kept a precarious neutral existence, an island of unoccupied ground ringed by Japanese-held territory, until Japan seized them after Pearl Harbor in December 1941.

ch04.note: The author; a Communist underground worker who from the 1920s to the 1940s ran united-front work with gang and secret-society figures in Beijing and Shanghai. His account is a rare inside record of how the Party used the gangs—candid about the transactional nature of the ties.

From Mao Zedong’s Analysis of the Classes in Chinese Society (1925). The passage on the ‘lumpen-proletariat’ and its secret societies—quoted here to license the Party’s use of the gangs—was among the lines Mao softened in later editions of his Selected Works.
1884–1951; also Hu Nanhu. A 1911 revolutionary and Beiyang education official who joined the Communist Party in the 1920s and worked its united front among old revolutionaries and gang figures.

1889–1927; co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party. In April 1927 Zhang Zuolin’s troops raided the Soviet embassy compound in Beijing’s Legation Quarter, where he had taken refuge, and hanged him—the event this passage describes.

Lev Karakhan (1889–1937), Soviet deputy foreign commissar and ambassador to China in the mid-1920s, known for the ‘Karakhan Manifesto’ renouncing Tsarist privileges. He was executed in Stalin’s purges.

Yang Du (1875–1931): the classical scholar who had once championed monarchy under Yuan Shikai, then joined the Communist Party in secret in 1929 while serving as an adviser to Du Yuesheng—a startling double life the Party did not confirm publicly until 1975. The book’s account of his role is broadly corroborated.

The walled diplomatic quarter of Beijing, established after 1901, where the foreign legations—including the Soviet embassy—enjoyed extraterritorial protection; Zhang Zuolin’s 1927 raid on the Soviet compound there breached that immunity.

The Mutual Aid Society (互济会) was the Chinese branch of International Red Aid, a Comintern body that supported jailed revolutionaries and their families. The organizer’s name is uncertain in the scan and is romanized here provisionally as Dai Xiaodong.
1889–1971; geologist and senior Nationalist official, acting president of Tsinghua University in 1931 and later premier; he returned to the mainland in 1951.

1882–1948; the ‘Christian general,’ a warlord whose loyalties shifted among the Nationalists, the Soviets, and the left. In 1933, with Communist help, he raised the short-lived Chahar People’s Anti-Japanese Allied Army at Zhangjiakou, into which the local forces described here were folded.

1915–1968; a Nationalist air-force bomber pilot who defected by flying his aircraft to the Communist base at Yan’an. His defection is dated June 1946 in the standard accounts; the article’s ‘1947’ appears to be a slip of memory.

76 Jessfield Road (极司非尔路, today Wanhangdu Road) was the headquarters of the secret service of the puppet Wang Jingwei regime, notorious for torture and assassination; its address became a synonym for the collaborationist terror apparatus.
1885–1961; a well-known Shanghai gang figure with revolutionary sympathies, treated at length in a later article of this volume.

1907–2000; Buddhist lay leader, poet, and relief organizer who used Shanghai’s charitable and refugee bodies to shelter and channel Communist work in the war years, and later headed the Buddhist Association of China. The refugee network he built here fed cadres to the New Fourth Army, as the article claims.

The Communist force operating in central and east China after 1937 under the united front, alongside the northern Eighth Route Army; the refugee schools and radio classes described here were among its recruiting grounds until the Nationalists attacked it in the 1941 New Fourth Army Incident.

The ‘Jiang-kang’ (江抗), an early Communist-influenced guerrilla force built in the Yangtze delta from local gang levies; reorganized under regular military command, it fed into the New Fourth Army’s eastward push.

ch05.anchor: ranked, by the order in which they entered, into twenty-four generations
ch05.note: The generation-characters are the key to Green Gang rank. Each member belonged to one of the twenty-four generations, named in fixed order by the characters of the verse; seniority ran by generation, not by age or wealth, so that a man of an earlier character outranked all of a later one. Thus of the late bosses, Zhang Renkui was of the ‘Da’ generation, Huang Jinrong of the ‘Tong,’ and Du Yuesheng of the ‘Wu’—Du being, in strict gang terms, junior to the other two.

Jiang Hao here sets down the gang’s own account of itself.

ch06.anchor: Tian Wenjing, was a Hangzhou man
ch06.note: Tian Wenjing (1662–1732) was a real and prominent Yongzheng-era governor of Henan; the gang legend attaches its founding to his sponsorship of a grain-transport reform.

The Eight Immortals, the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the thirty-six Heavenly Stars, and the seventy-two Earthly Fiends are stock numbers of Chinese cosmology and popular fiction (the thirty-six and seventy-two are the number of the bandit-heroes of Water Margin); the legend borrows them for the founders’ first intakes of disciples.
The ‘Mandarin Duck and Butterfly’ school was a popular current of sentimental and romantic fiction in early-Republican Shanghai, looked down on by the new-literature writers.
Kawashima Yoshiko (1907–1948), a Manchu Qing princess raised in Japan who worked as a Japanese agent; executed as a traitor after the war.
No. 76 Jessfield Road was the notorious headquarters of the secret service of the puppet Wang Jingwei regime during the occupation, a byword for terror and torture.

The Juntong (军统), the Nationalists’ Bureau of Investigation and Statistics, the Kuomintang secret service run by Dai Li. The English form is not yet settled across this series and is treated fully at the chapter on Du Yuesheng’s ties to Dai Li; here it is rendered ‘the Juntong.’

ch06.anchor: his organization was called the Yi Society, and in the Hongmen he was lord of the Wuxing Mountain lodge
ch06.note: Several minor Shanghai clubs bore near-homophonous names all rendered ‘Yi Society’ here: Zhu Xuefan’s 毅社 (Chapter 3), Xu Yimin’s 逸社, and Sun Yixiang’s 怔社—distinct bodies that happen to sound alike.

ch06.anchor: the noted film actress Ruan Lingyu
ch06.note: Ruan Lingyu (1910–1935), one of the great stars of Shanghai silent film, whose suicide at twenty-four was a national sensation.
Silas Aaron Hardoon (1851–1931), a Baghdadi-Jewish property magnate, reputedly the richest foreigner in Shanghai; his wife Luo Jialing (Liza Hardoon) was Eurasian.

ch06.anchor: one of the "Three Big Bosses" among the Shanghai gangsters
ch06.note: The ‘Three Big Bosses’ (san da heng) of the Shanghai underworld—Huang Jinrong, Zhang Xiaolin, and Du Yuesheng—the trio around whom much of this book turns.
The ‘CC Clique,’ the Kuomintang organizational faction led by the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, a mainstay of anti-Communist party control.

ch07.anchor: the Three Harmonies Society, the Elder Brothers Society
ch07.note: The Hongmen (洪门) was less a single body than a family of sworn-brotherhood secret societies. The Heaven and Earth Society (天地会, Tiandihui), the Three Harmonies Society (三合会, Sanhehui—the "Triads" of Western usage), and the Elder Brothers Society (哥老会, Gelaohui, strong in the upper Yangtze) were its principal branches. On the distinction between the Hongmen and the Green Gang, see the note at the head of the book.

ch07.anchor: Legend gives its first ancestor as Hong Ying
ch07.note: The origin story that follows—Hong Ying and the loyalist scholars, the Shaolin monk-soldiers, the burning of the temple, the Five Ancestors, the oath at the Red Flower Pavilion—is the Hongmen's own traditional founding myth, not history, and its names, dates, and battles are uncorroborated. Modern scholarship traces the Tiandihui to actual sworn brotherhoods in Fujian in the mid-eighteenth century (Qianlong reign); the earlier Ming-loyalist pedigree was grafted on later to give the society an anti-Manchu ancestry. As with the parallel Green Gang genealogy (see the preceding chapters), the legend is rendered here as the source gives it.

ch07.anchor: transferred his allegiance to Shi Kefa
ch07.note: Shi Kefa (1601–1645), the Ming grand secretary and commander who died defending Yangzhou against the Qing conquest and became the great symbol of Ming loyalist resistance—a real figure woven into the legend.

ch07.anchor: followed Zheng Chenggong in holding Taiwan
ch07.note: Zheng Chenggong (1624–1662), known in the West as Koxinga: the Ming loyalist sea-lord who drove the Dutch from Taiwan in 1662 and held it against the Qing. The Hongmen legend adopts him as the founder of its first "mountain" and "hall."

ch07.anchor: the Red Flower Pavilion in Xiaputan
ch07.note: The oath at the Red Flower Pavilion (红花亭) is the Hongmen's mythic founding assembly. The splitting of the surname-character 洪 (Hong) into the strokes "three, eight, twenty-one" was a genuine Hongmen recognition-cipher, used, as the text later explains, in passwords and on ritual objects.

ch07.anchor: In 1893, in Honolulu in the United States
ch07.note: Sun Yat-sen's tie to the Hongmen is well attested: he was initiated into the overseas brotherhood (the Chee Kung Tong / Hongmen) and drew on its members and its funds through the early risings, formally taking a Hongmen "Red Staff" rank in Honolulu in 1904. The dates and details here are the author's; the essential fact—that the republican revolution leaned heavily on the Hongmen abroad—is corroborated.

ch07.anchor: the Empress Dowager Cixi's seventieth birthday
ch07.note: Cixi (1835–1908), the Empress Dowager who dominated the late Qing court for nearly half a century. Her seventieth-birthday celebrations fell in the winter of 1904; the plotters meant to strike while officialdom was absorbed in the "Longevity Festival."

ch07.anchor: Expel the Manchu barbarians, restore China, found a republic, and equalize land rights
ch07.note: The famous four-point program of the Revolutionary Alliance (Tongmenghui), founded in Tokyo in 1905. The account here telescopes two things: the 1905 Tokyo founding under Sun Yat-sen, and the 1911 Central China Bureau of the Alliance, set up at Hankou under Song Jiaoren—which is what the "central bureau" and Song's management actually refer to.

ch07.anchor: the Yellow Flower Mound affair of April 1911
ch07.note: The Huanghuagang uprising at Guangzhou, 27 April 1911, in which many revolutionaries died; its "seventy-two martyrs" became a revered symbol. It was the last of the pre-1911 risings before the Wuchang rising that October brought down the dynasty.

ch07.anchor: the four characters "fan you fu lei,"
ch07.note: The altar objects encode the society's aim by homophone and rebus: 反油复泪 (fan you fu lei) stands for 反清复明 (fan Qing fu Ming), "overthrow the Qing and restore the Ming." This restorationist slogan—whatever the members' actual conduct—defined the Hongmen's self-image against the Green Gang, which had served the Qing grain transport.
Chen Qimei (1878–1916), revolutionary organizer, military governor of Shanghai in 1911, and an early patron of Chiang Kai-shek. He was assassinated in Shanghai in 1916 on Yuan Shikai's orders.

The rising aboard the cruiser Zhaohe (肇和) in Shanghai, December 1915, an attempt led by Chen Qimei against Yuan Shikai's monarchy; Yang Hu took part. It failed, but the naval mutinies of these years were an important thread of the anti-Yuan struggle.

ch07.anchor: the noted Hongmen man Xu Langxi
ch07.note: Xu Langxi (1885–1961), a Shaanxi revolutionary, Tongmenghui member, and Hongmen leader who founded the Xinhua Art School in Shanghai. A later chapter of this book is his son's memoir of him.
See the note on the Small Sword Society's 1853 seizure of the Shanghai county city, earlier in the book.

Situ Meitang (1868–1955), the most celebrated overseas-Chinese Hongmen leader, long the head of the Chee Kung Tong in the United States; he supported the republican revolution and the war of resistance, and after 1949 helped found the China Zhi Gong Party. His visit to Shanghai in 1946 is the occasion of the convention described here.

ch08.anchor: Before liberation I worked in the French Concession police for more than twenty years
ch08.note: The author, Xue Gengshen, rose to be the most senior Chinese detective—chief inspector, and finally special-grade chief inspector—of the French Concession police, and after 1949 set down several memoirs of the Shanghai underworld he had policed for it. His surname is brushed on the byline with the variant graph 畊 for 耕.

ch08.anchor: Zhang Renkui, styled Jinhu
ch08.note: Zhang Renkui (1865–1944), a patriarch of the Green Gang's senior "Da" generation and a warlord-era garrison commander at Tonghai in Jiangsu, whose disciples ran into the tens of thousands. A later chapter of this book is devoted to him and his Ren Society.

ch08.anchor: the late-Qing top graduate Zhang Jian
ch08.note: Zhang Jian (1853–1926), the zhuangyuan (first-place metropolitan graduate) of 1894 who turned industrialist and built the pioneering Dasheng cotton mills at Nantong—hence the purchase of British mill machinery here.

ch08.anchor: a man dreads fame as a pig dreads getting fat
ch08.note: A common proverb (人怕出名猪怕壮): a fattened pig is the one taken to slaughter, and fame, like fatness, invites destruction.

ch08.anchor: the Kuomintang elder Yu Youren
ch08.note: Yu Youren (1879–1964), a founding revolutionary, renowned calligrapher, and long-serving president of the Control Yuan of the Nationalist government.

ch08.anchor: over the famous actress Lu Lanchun
ch08.note: The Huang Jinrong–Lu Lanchun affair of the early 1920s: Huang, infatuated with the opera actress Lu Lanchun, clashed with Lu Xiaojia, son of the Zhejiang warlord Lu Yongxiang, was seized and publicly humiliated, and had to be ransomed—a loss of face that is usually reckoned the turning point after which Du Yuesheng eclipsed him.

ch08.anchor: in the campaign to suppress counterrevolutionaries
ch08.note: The nationwide campaign to suppress counterrevolutionaries (镇反) of 1950–1951, under which many former gangsters and collaborators were tried; "lifelong control" (管制) was a supervised-residence penalty short of prison.

ch08.anchor: through Yu Qiaqing's introduction
ch08.note: Yu Qiaqing (1867–1945), the leading Ningbo comprador-financier of Shanghai and a president of its General Chamber of Commerce; a major thoroughfare, today's Xizang Road, was for a time named for him.

ch08.anchor: what is colloquially called "planting lotus."
ch08.note: Gangland slang (种荷花) for drowning a victim, weighted, off the mouth of the Wusong. The murder recounted here—of a pregnant dance-hall girl carrying the child of a member of the Soong family—rests on the author's word alone; he presents it as a secret he was sworn to keep, and it is uncorroborated by any outside source.

ch08.anchor: manager of the Great World
ch08.note: The Great World (大世界), the sprawling amusement hall opened on Avenue Édouard VII in 1917, Shanghai's most famous popular entertainment palace and long a prize the gangs fought over.

ch08.anchor: it touched the affairs of the Soong family
ch08.note: The Soong (宋) family, at the summit of Nationalist power: Song Ziliang was a younger brother of the financier T. V. Soong (Song Ziwen) and of Soong Ai-ling, Soong Ching-ling, and Soong Mei-ling (Madame Chiang). The story is single-source; see the preceding note.

ch08.anchor: his name was Lin Huaibu (nicknamed
ch08.note: The assassination of Zhang Xiaolin on 14 August 1940 is recounted, consistently, in an earlier chapter of this book: killed at his window by his own bodyguard Lin Huaibu on the Juntong's order, on the pretext of his coming defection to the Japanese puppets. The two accounts agree on the killer and the Juntong's hand.

ch08.anchor: the Subei Native-Place Association
ch08.note: "Jiangbei" or "Subei" is the poorer country north of the Yangtze in Jiangsu; its migrants formed a large, looked-down-on laboring underclass in Shanghai, and to call a man a "Jiangbei big boss" carried that edge. Native-place associations organized such migrant communities—and, in the underworld, their manpower.

ch08.anchor: Shi Qian of Water Margin
ch08.note: Shi Qian, the "Flea on a Drum" of the classic novel Water Margin, a nimble burglar among the Liangshan outlaws—the natural patron for a guild of thieves.

ch08.anchor: the "Ten Brave Men of China,"
ch08.note: "China" here renders 支那 (Shina), the name Japan used for China in this period, by then heard as a deliberate slur. The episode of the ten tortured Miao resisters, honored by their killers, is the author's account.

ch08.anchor: lured by the "yellow-croaker" method
ch08.note: "Yellow-croaker dealing" (贩黄鱼) was cant for smuggling people: as the text explains, a Chinese who died in transit was thrown overboard "like a fish." The racket ran Qingtian stone-carvers and bound-foot women through Portugal into France.

ch08.anchor: Opium was of four grades: "Indian earth,"
ch08.note: The opium grades named the source: "Indian earth" (imported), and the domestic "Yunnan earth," "Sichuan earth," and "Mongol earth." Home-grown opium was a mainstay of warlord finance in the southwest and northwest, which is why the trade and the militarists were inseparable.

ch08.anchor: the China-destroying apparatus led by Toyama Mitsuru
ch08.note: The Black Dragon Society (黑龙会, Kokuryūkai), a Japanese ultranationalist and expansionist organization; Toyama Mitsuru (1855–1944) was the veteran éminence grise of the pan-Asianist secret-society world behind it.

ch08.anchor: who took Chu Minyi as his adoptive father
ch08.note: Chu Minyi (1884–1946), foreign minister of the Wang Jingwei collaborationist regime, executed as a traitor after the war; Ding Mocun (1901–1947), a chief of the regime's secret police, likewise executed. To claim either as patron or backer was to stand openly with the occupation.

ch08.anchor: founded the "Yiyuan greyhound track" and a "jai alai fronton"
ch08.note: Jai alai (回力球), the fast Basque ball game, was run as a betting spectacle at the Auditorium in the French Concession; with the greyhound tracks and the racecourse it made up the settlements' legal-gambling apparatus.

ch08.anchor: the staff of the French police and the Mixed Court
ch08.note: The Mixed Court (会审公堂), the tribunal in the foreign settlements in which a Chinese magistrate sat with a foreign assessor—an instrument of extraterritorial control over Chinese residents until it was returned to Chinese authority in the later 1920s.

ch08.anchor: the freight charge ran from ten to twenty-five cents in fabi
ch08.note: Fabi (法币), the Nationalist government's managed paper currency, introduced in the 1935 currency reform in place of the silver dollar.

ch08.anchor: had foreigners and their "second devils" to back them
ch08.note: "Second devils" (二鬼子), a contemptuous term for Chinese who served foreign masters as enforcers or agents—the foreigners being the "foreign devils."

ch08.anchor: so touching off the January 28 Shanghai resistance war
ch08.note: The January 28 Incident of 1932 (一二八): Japanese forces attacked Chinese-held Zhabei, and the 19th Route Army fought them for weeks. The burning of the Sanyou Industrial Company—a firm effective in the boycott of Japanese goods—was one of the provocations that set it off.

ch08.anchor: Lu Bohong, general manager of the Nanshi Water and Electric Company
ch08.note: Lu Bohong (1875–1937), a prominent Catholic industrialist and philanthropist of Shanghai. He was assassinated in December 1937; the attribution of the killing to the Juntong's Chen Mo, and the charge that he had been bought by Chang Yuqing, are the author's.

ch09.anchor: In his later years he organized the Ren Society in Shanghai
ch09.note: The Ren Society (仁社), founded by Zhang Renkui in 1935, was one of the disciple-fraternities the Shanghai bosses set up on the model of a modern club to bind their followings together, alongside Huang Jinrong's Rong Society and Du Yuesheng's Heng Society (the last is the subject of ch20 and its charter is appended). For Zhang Renkui himself see the note at ch08.

ch09.anchor: the bomb blew him to pieces
ch09.note: The salt-bandit Xu Baoshan (徐宝山) was in fact killed by a bomb hidden in a curio case on 24 May 1913 — during the “Second Revolution” against Yuan Shikai, not, as the surrounding passage implies, during the 1911 Revolution itself. Contemporary accounts credit the assassination to the revolutionaries around Chen Qimei, who had the bomb-maker plant it in an antique Xu had agreed to buy; the book's outline of the method is otherwise correct.

The dou here (颗当, a gang term) mark seniority by the Green Gang's twenty-four generation-characters, the fixed sequence that fixes every member's rank; the ordering is explained in the note at ch05. To “wear the twenty-four” was to stand at the top of that ladder.

ch09.anchor: took Zhang Jian as his teacher
ch09.note: Zhang Jian (张謇, 1853–1926), the Nantong-born reformer, top graduate (zhuangyuan) of the 1894 palace examination, and pioneer industrialist whose Dasheng cotton mills, schools and land-reclamation works made Nantong a model town. “Haonan Villa” (濠南别业) was his Nantong residence, now a museum. That a salt-smuggler-turned-garrison-commander should court him as a teacher shows how far Zhang Renkui sought respectability.
Zhang Cha (张詧), Zhang Jian's elder brother and partner in his enterprises; “Mr. Zhang the Third” reflects his rank among the wider cousinry, not among his own siblings.

Zhao Dan (赵丹, 1915–1980) became one of China's most celebrated film actors (Crossroads, Street Angel, The Lin Family Shop). His father, here named Zhao Zichao, was indeed a military man of the warlord years who later ran cinemas at Nantong; the detail of his service under Zhang Renkui is the memoirist's own.

ch09.anchor: Chen Guangfu, general manager of the Shanghai Commercial Bank
ch09.note: Chen Guangfu (陈光甫, 1881–1976), known in the West as K. P. Chen, founder and head of the Shanghai Commercial and Savings Bank and the most respected Chinese banker of the Republican era. His appearance here as a man forced to seek gang protection over a private scandal shows how far the underworld's reach ran into respectable finance.

ch09.anchor: chairman of the management committee of the Jiaoji Railway
ch09.note: Ge Guangting (葛光庭) is named here as a Japanese-trained Beiyang veteran and Ren Society member; his identity as chairman of the Jiaoji (Qingdao–Jinan) Railway committee and graduate of the Japanese Military Academy could not be independently confirmed, and is given as the memoirist reports it.

ch09.anchor: stabbed to death at home by his own bodyguard
ch09.note: Zhang Xiaoruo (张孝若, 1898–1935), Zhang Jian's only son and his successor in the Dasheng enterprises, was shot dead by his own servant Wu Yigao at his Shanghai residence on 17 October 1935; the servant then killed himself, and the motive was never established.

Han Fuju (韩复榘, 1890–1938), a general who rose under Feng Yuxiang and became governor of Shandong; Chiang Kai-shek had him executed in 1938 for abandoning the province to the Japanese without a fight. “Xiangfang” (向方) was his style-name.

ch09.anchor: they had to welcome the Great Dragon Head
ch09.note: The “Great Dragon Head” (大龙头) is a supreme secret-society chief. This tale of Zuo Zongtang's army halting at Pingliang to receive one, and of Zuo himself later taking a gang master, is Green Gang oral legend meant to dignify the brotherhood; it is not found in the historical record of Zuo's 1870s Xinjiang campaign and should be read as lore, not fact.

ch09.anchor: one Jiang Dingwen, the other Zhu Shaoliang
ch09.note: Both were senior Nationalist generals: Jiang Dingwen (蒋鼎文, 1895–1974) and Zhu Shaoliang (朱绍良, 1891–1963), each of whom held front commands and provincial governorships. That such men sought a gang elder's card is the point the memoirist is making about Zhang Renkui's standing.

ch09.anchor: going in for "three knives and six holes"
ch09.note: “Three knives and six holes” (三刀六洞) is gang shorthand for a violent ordeal or punishment — a man stabbed through so that each of three thrusts leaves an entry and an exit wound — used both to test nerve and to settle scores. Chen's boast is that his lower-tier disciples are the muscle, as against the “refined” front men the narrator usually meets.

ch09.anchor: to lure and seize its chairman, Wang Shouhua
ch09.note: Wang Shouhua (汪寿华, 1901–1927), a Communist and chairman of the Shanghai General Labor Union, was lured to Du Yuesheng's house on the night of 11 April 1927 and murdered there — the opening act of the April 12 purge (see the note at ch02). His killing recurs, from the gangsters' side, in ch12.

ch09.anchor: much of the "strength of the North" about him
ch09.note: An allusion to the Doctrine of the Mean, which contrasts the “strength of the South” (forbearance) with the “strength of the North” (unflinching hardness, “to lie under arms and die without regret”). Applied to Zhang Renkui it marks him as a hard northern soldier.

ch10.anchor: Yuan Hanyun, whose given name was Kewen
ch10.note: Yuan Kewen (袁克文, 1889–1931), hao Hanyun, second son of Yuan Shikai: a poet, calligrapher, coin- and jade-collector, Kunqu amateur and famous spendthrift who openly opposed his father's imperial venture. A Green Gang “Da”-generation celebrity, he died in poverty at Tianjin in 1931, his funeral — the memoir's subject remembers — paid for by friends and thronged by the city's singsong girls.

ch10.anchor: the second son of Yuan Shikai
ch10.note: Yuan Shikai (袁世凯, 1859–1916), the Beiyang army-builder who became the Republic's first president in 1912 and then had himself proclaimed emperor at the end of 1915; the monarchy collapsed within months amid nationwide revolt, and he died in June 1916. His household politics drive this whole chapter.

Yuan Keding (袁克定, 1878–1955), Yuan Shikai's eldest son and the chief pusher of the monarchy, in which he expected to be crown prince. Lame from a riding accident, he is notorious for having a counterfeit edition of the Shuntian Times printed daily to feed his father only pro-monarchy news — the deception the narrator alludes to below.

“Wanhua” (畹华) was the style-name of Mei Lanfang (梅兰芳, 1894–1961), the supreme dan (female-role) actor of Peking opera, whose art carried the form to Japan, the United States and the Soviet Union. His friendship with the opera-loving Yuan Kewen is well documented.

ch10.anchor: On the very morning Duan Qirui went to Xiaozhan
ch10.note: Duan Qirui (段祺瑞, 1865–1936), one of Yuan Shikai's original Xiaozhan-era commanders and later premier and Beiyang strongman; he broke with Yuan over the monarchy. Xiaozhan, near Tianjin, was where Yuan had drilled his New Army in the 1890s. The anecdote of Yuan Keding's insult (“I grant you a seat”) driving Duan to raise troops is the memoirist's; Duan's opposition to the monarchy is well attested.

ch10.anchor: the Shuntian Times, I published an article
ch10.note: The Shuntian Times (顺天时报) was an influential Japanese-run Chinese-language daily in Beijing. Its independence is what made Yuan Keding's forged in-house edition necessary; that Yuan Kewen used the real paper to publish against the monarchy sharpened the family quarrel he describes.

ch10.anchor: a rectangular seal of four characters, 'the Sovereign's Second Son,'
ch10.note: Yuan Kewen is famous for signing himself the “Imperial Second Son” (皇二子); the seal here is given in the memoir as four characters, 上第二子, “the Sovereign's Second Son” (上 standing for the emperor). Stamped on his books, it was his father's way of marking him as untouchable while spiriting him out of the capital.

ch10.anchor: 'honor the patriarch' before your Grandfather Zhang
ch10.note: To “honor the patriarch” (孝祖) is to enter the Green Gang by doing formal obeisance before the founding masters — often, as here, before a deceased master's tablet. Yuan speaks in gang-kinship banter: because his listener Chen is Yuan's own disciple, Yuan's gang-master ranks as Chen's “grandfather,” hence “your Grandfather Zhang.”

ch10.anchor: When Zhang Zongchang came to Beijing
ch10.note: Zhang Zongchang (张宗昌, 1881–1932), the “Dogmeat General,” warlord of Shandong under the Zhili–Shandong alliance, notorious for his brutality, his concubines and his doggerel verse. He was assassinated in 1932.

The Crystal (晶报), founded 1919 and appearing every three days, was the most celebrated of Shanghai's “mosquito papers” — small sheets of gossip, anecdote and society news. Yuan Kewen was one of its star contributors; his serialized reminiscences of the Beiyang court helped make its name. Its editor-manager was Yu Daxiong.

ch10.anchor: This was what was then called the way of the "man about town."
ch10.note: “Man about town” renders baixiangren (白相人), Shanghai slang for a well-connected idler who lives by his contacts and his wits — the milieu of favors, face and free performances the passage describes.

ch10.anchor: play old Tang in Beheading Tang
ch10.note: Beheading Tang (审头刺汤, “Examining the Head and Stabbing Tang”) is a Peking-opera piece of intrigue and revenge; “old Tang” is the villain Tang Qin, a comic-villain (chou) role. Yuan Kewen was a noted amateur of exactly this part.

ch10.anchor: Zhang Zongchang made Teacher Hanyun "Commander of the Advance Army"
ch10.note: This appointment, and the elaborate but hollow “Advance Army headquarters” the chapter goes on to describe, rest on the memoirist's account; no independent record of Zhang Zongchang naming Yuan Kewen an army commander has been found, and the honor was plainly a sinecure traded on his name.

The third son, Yuan Jialiu (袁家骝, 1912–2003), became the distinguished physicist known in the West as Luke Chia-Liu Yuan, a specialist in high-energy accelerators; in 1942 he married the physicist Chien-Shiung Wu (吴健雄), the “first lady of physics.” His father's judgment proved sound.

ch11.anchor: My late father Xu Langxi was born in 1885
ch11.note: For Xu Langxi (徐朗西, 1885–1961) — Shaanxi revolutionary, Tongmenghui member, Hongmen leader and art educator — see the notes at ch07 and ch04. This article is written by his son and, dating from 1986, dwells on his ties to the Communist underground; the account is affectionate and should be read as a family memoir, sound in outline but weighted, in places, toward its subject's later loyalties.

ch11.anchor: When he organized the Revive China Society in Tokyo
ch11.note: This misremembers the founding: Sun Yat-sen's Revive China Society (兴中会) was set up in Honolulu (1894) and Hong Kong (1895); the body founded at Tokyo in 1905 was the larger Revolutionary Alliance (Tongmenghui). Sun's own tie to the secret societies is real, however: he was initiated into the Chee Kung Tong (a Hongmen lodge) at Honolulu on 11 January 1904.

ch11.anchor: the Qing, the Hong, the Li, and the Bai are all revolutionary bodies
ch11.note: The dictum groups the secret brotherhoods — the Qing (Green) Gang, the Hongmen, and the smaller Li and Bai currents — as fellow anti-Qing bodies. It is widely attributed to Sun Yat-sen but is hard to pin to a exact passage of the Three People's Principles; take the attribution as the tradition of the gangs' own literature rather than a verified quotation.

ch11.anchor: the Japanese Toyama Mitsuru and Miyazaki Torazo
ch11.note: Toyama Mitsuru (头山满, 1855–1944), the pan-Asianist and founder of the Gen'yōsha, and Miyazaki Tōten (宫崎寅藏, 1871–1922), the “benefactor of the Chinese republic” who introduced Sun to Huang Xing and Song Jiaoren, were the two Japanese most closely tied to Sun's movement and, through it, to the Chinese secret societies.

This conference of the Hongmen's nine “Great Dragon Heads,” called to modernize the brotherhood's feudal usages, is reported only in this family memoir; no independent record of it has been found, and it should be treated as the memoirist's account.

ch11.anchor: the Jingguo Army under Yu Youren to answer the call
ch11.note: In 1918 an anti-Duan “Constitution-Protection” rising at Sanyuan formed the Shaanxi Jingguo (“pacify-the-nation”) Army against the Beiyang governor Chen Shufan; Yu Youren (于右任, 1879–1964), the poet, calligrapher and revolutionary, returned to head it, while Tang Jiyao of Yunnan led the wider allied command. This framework is well attested; Xu Langxi's personal role as vanguard commander rests on his son's account.

ch11.anchor: the four great characters "The world belongs to all."
ch11.note: “The world belongs to all” (天下为公, tianxia wei gong), from the “Liyun” chapter of the Book of Rites, was Sun Yat-sen's signature inscription, brushed for countless followers; its use as a personal keepsake here is entirely in character.

ch11.anchor: introduced three Kuomintang Juntong underground agents
ch11.note: That Xu Langxi personally introduced these three named agents to the collaborator Zhou Fohai, and fed the resulting intelligence to the Communist underground, is the son's claim and has not been independently corroborated. Its general shape is plausible: Zhou Fohai did run a documented secret channel to Dai Li's Juntong and Chongqing from about 1943, “surrendering” to the Nationalists in 1945. On the standing of the Juntong (军统) see the note at ch06.

ch11.anchor: found a library at the Chinese Academy of Fine Arts
ch11.note: Xu Langxi was a founder and head of an early private art college in Shanghai (associated with Liu Haisu and Wang Yachen, and usually named as the Xinhua Academy of Fine Arts); the exact name given here, the Chinese Academy of Fine Arts (中华艺术专科学校), is left as printed.

ch11.anchor: Yu Youren and Dai Chuanxian even came in person
ch11.note: Dai Chuanxian (戴传贤, 1891–1949) is the Nationalist elder better known as Dai Jitao, ideologue and long-serving president of the Examination Yuan. “Chen Yingshi,” named just below as an early sworn brother of Xu's and of Chiang's, is Chen Qimei (see the note at ch07); Yu Youren, nicknamed “the Beard,” was then president of the Control Yuan, the barb behind Xu's retort about “Long live the Generalissimo.”

ch12.note: This life of Huang Jinrong (黄金荣, 1868–1953; see also the note at ch02) is reprinted from a Republican-history biographical series and is written in an openly hostile, prosecutorial key, unlike the household memoirs that follow. Its outline is sound — Suzhou birth, a constable father, a French Concession police career, retirement in the mid-1920s as the force's only Chinese chief inspector — though sources put his entry into the police variously at 1892 or 1894.

The “Thirty-Six Gang,” “Eight Gang” and “Hundred and Eight Generals” (the last echoing the outlaw-heroes of the Water Margin) are the standard furniture of Shanghai gang recollection — Huang's networks of informers and enforcers — but they are descriptive lore rather than externally documented bodies.

ch12.anchor: sent Gao Xinbao, who had ties to the Lake Tai bandit chiefs, to "pay respects to the mountain."
ch12.note: To “pay respects to the mountain” (拜山) is to approach a bandit chief through the etiquette of the brotherhoods. This rescue of a French consular clerk's wife kidnapped at Lake Tai is a memoir anecdote, told to Huang's credit; no independent record of it has been found.

ch12.anchor: the Green Gang "Da"-generation man Zhang Jinghu
ch12.note: “Zhang Jinghu” is Zhang Renkui, whose hao appears here as Jinghu (镜湖) though ch08 and ch09 give it as Jinhu (锦湖) — one of the book's own small inconsistencies, left as printed. The passage confirms from the other side what ch09 relates: Huang, never formally initiated, paid Zhang 20,000 yuan late in life to buy the “Tong”-generation standing he had long claimed.

ch12.anchor: Chiang sent Yang Hu, Chen Qun, and Wang Bailing
ch12.note: Chiang Kai-shek's three agents for the Shanghai purge: Yang Hu (杨虎), head of the garrison's secret-police apparatus (see ch08); Chen Qun (陈群), political-department director and later a Wang Jingwei-regime official; and Wang Bailing (王柏龄), deputy commander of the First Army. Bai Chongxi (白崇禧), named below, held the Shanghai garrison command during the coup. Their roles are well attested.

The China Mutual Progress Society (中华共进会) was the front organization through which the gangs' gunmen were marshalled for the April 12 purge; it drew on Green and Hong Gang manpower under Nationalist direction.

“Learning, conduct, loyalty, faith” (文行忠信) are the four things Confucius is said in the Analects to have taught — an incongruously scholarly motto for a gangster's pleasure-garden, and a mark of how far Chiang went to flatter his useful ally.

ch12.anchor: the great Shanghai pigment merchant Bei
ch12.note: The Bei (贝) family were among Shanghai's wealthiest, their fortune founded on the pigment and dyestuffs trade; the architect I. M. Pei was of this line. A kidnapping of one of their children, brokered by Huang for a ransom, epitomizes the “protection” racket the passage describes.

The Great World (大世界), opened 1917 near Avenue Edward VII, was Shanghai's largest popular entertainment complex — a multi-storey warren of opera stages, sideshows, food and games. Huang controlled it; his refusal to give it over as a refugee shelter in 1937 is offered as a measure of the man.

ch12.anchor: the Japanese naval attaché's office in China sent Rear Admiral Satō
ch12.note: The standard account of Huang Jinrong's war is the one implied here: unlike his fellow boss Zhang Xiaolin, who went over to the Japanese and was assassinated for it in 1940, Huang stayed in Shanghai, kept a low profile, and declined to head a puppet government. The specific 1938 overture by a Rear Admiral Satō, and the terms said to have been agreed, rest on this account; his followers' drift into collaborationist posts, described next, is not in doubt.

ch12.anchor: his disciple Hao Pengju was security commander of Huaihai province
ch12.note: Hao Pengju (郝鹏举, 1903–1947) was the era's most notorious turncoat, changing sides among the Nationalists, the Xi'an mutineers, the Japanese-puppet forces, the Nationalists again, and finally the Communists; the Communists captured and executed him in 1947. Li Changjiang (李长江), named just below, defected with his troops to the Japanese in February 1941, prompting the New Fourth Army's “punish Li Changjiang” campaign.

ch12.anchor: Ding Mocun, and its minister of industry and commerce, Mei Siping
ch12.note: Ding Mocun (丁默村, 1901–1947), a former Communist turned Nationalist secret-policeman turned Wang Jingwei minister of social affairs and secret-service chief; and Mei Siping (梅思平, 1896–1946), the regime's minister of industry (later interior). Both were tried and shot as traitors after the war.

ch12.anchor: buy houses and property in Hong Kong, Macao, and elsewhere.
ch12.note: Editors' note. According to recollection, it was Li Zhiqing who made off with Huang's rolled-up valuables; see Cheng's article in this volume.

ch12.anchor: Huang Jinrong publicly confessed his crimes in the press
ch12.note: This refers to Huang's famous self-criticism (自白书), published in the Shanghai press in May 1951, after which the aged boss was set to sweeping the street outside his own Great World as a public spectacle. He died in Shanghai in 1953. The People's Government's “lenient treatment” spared him the fate of many lesser figures.

ch12.anchor: Draft Historical Materials of the Republic of China
ch12.note: The source, Zhonghua minguo shi ziliao congkao (中华民国史资料丛稿), was a mainland scholarly series of Republican-era historical materials; this biography is a reprint from its “Biographies” section, lightly revised for the present volume.

ch13.note: Author’s note: “Bairen” (‘men about town’) was pre-1949 Shanghai slang for gang and hoodlum types. Besides Xue Liansheng, the ‘Five-Sheng Party’ were the dentist Chen Runsheng, the toyshop keeper Wang Tingsheng, the lime-shop keeper Shen Jusheng, and Zhu Yousheng, who later managed the City God Temple’s incense money. — The name puns on the character sheng (‘born’) shared by all five.

ch13.anchor: the Sanxin Company (the headquarters of the whole Shanghai opium trade)
ch13.note: The Sanxin (‘Three Prosperities’) Company, founded in the early 1920s, was the cartel through which Huang Jinrong, Du Yuesheng and Zhang Xiaolin monopolized the French Concession opium traffic under police protection. It is the engine of the three bosses’ fortunes throughout this book; its workings are described in section VII.

A gang nickname for the first cohort of Chinese plainclothes detectives Huang joined in the French police. Gudang (‘share party’) is the recurring gang term for a band that divided its spoils in shares; the ‘Big’ and ‘Little Eight-Share Parties’ and the ‘Thirty-Six-Share Party’ below are the same formation on a larger scale.

The French Concession police employed Vietnamese (‘Annamese,’ from the French protectorate of Annam) as uniformed constables, a common colonial practice of using one subject people to police another. A personal guard of them was a mark of Huang’s standing.

Rong Desheng (1875–1952) was a leading cotton-and-flour industrialist. He was in fact kidnapped in Shanghai in 1946—late in Huang’s life, not in his rise—and his family was extorted of more than 600,000 US dollars, most of it by Nationalist officials rather than by Huang’s men. The steward’s attribution of the affair to Huang’s disciple Ding Yongchang is uncorroborated and at odds with the usual accounts; it reads as gang lore folded into Huang’s early career. (Corroboration: contradicted.)

ch13.anchor: the kidnapping of the French Bishop Yao
ch13.note: The historical event this echoes is the Lincheng Outrage of 5–6 May 1923, when bandits under Sun Meiyao derailed the ‘Blue Express’ near Lincheng in Shandong and held twenty-six foreigners and over a hundred Chinese for thirty-seven days before their release that June. It was not the work of Zhang Zongchang’s troops, and no French bishop figures in the record. Huang’s account of single-handedly ransoming a ‘Bishop Yao’ on a stray tip is uncorroborated and conflates the famous train affair with gang legend. (Corroboration: uncorroborated / contradicted.)

ch13.anchor: escorted the City God's image out of the temple
ch13.note: The City God (Chenghuang) is the tutelary deity of a walled town; his temple was the ceremonial and social heart of the old Chinese city, and his image was carried in procession on festival days. Huang’s presidency of its incense-society marks how far a French-police detective stood inside popular religious life.

ch13.anchor: through the introduction of Huang's disciple Xu Fusheng
ch13.note: This whole account of Huang’s aid to Sun Yat-sen—the fan-leaves, the thousand yuan, the letters signed “Sun Wen”—rests on Huang’s own telling on the opium couch and on his disciples’ recollection, with no independent record. Sun did use Shanghai’s gang world, but Huang’s claim to have bankrolled the revolution is self-serving and unverified. (Corroboration: uncorroborated.)

The two memoirs disagree over Lu Lanchun’s later life: this steward’s account has her marry the laosheng singer An Shuyuan and then a dyestuffs comprador surnamed Xue, and gives her age at marriage to Huang as twenty-four; the following chapter names only An Shuyuan and differs on the dates. Both are rendered as printed.

Pingtan is the Suzhou-dialect storytelling-and-ballad art, sung to a pipa and sanxian; the Tale of Yue Fei was a staple of its repertoire, which is why the loyal general’s story could move Huang as it does here.

Wang Bamei (‘Eighth Sister Wang’) was a woman guerrilla leader in the Lake Tai region during the war; “Two-Gun” (shuangqiang) is the stock epithet for such a fighter. Her band’s rescue of a downed American pilot is the kind of episode Huang’s people cultivated to keep a foot in every camp.

Chiang Ching-kuo’s 1948 ‘tiger-beating’ campaign in Shanghai—enforcing the new gold-yuan currency and cracking down on speculators and hoarders—briefly jailed even Du Yuesheng’s son Du Weiping. It collapsed within months as inflation ran away.

ch14.note: Editors’ note: this account is inaccurate; see Cheng Xiwen’s article — that is, the preceding chapter, whose steward gives Huang two brothers and two sisters. —Eds.

Editors’ note: one account gives her as Lin Guisheng. —Eds. The preceding chapter (Cheng Xiwen’s) names Huang’s first wife Lin Guisheng, and later Republican-era scholarship favours Lin; this narrator gives Ye. Rendered as each writer prints it.

The ‘solitary island’ (gudao) is the standard name for the period from the fall of Chinese Shanghai in November 1937 to Pearl Harbor in December 1941, when the foreign concessions carried on as an enclave surrounded by Japanese-occupied territory—a lawless interval in which gangs and puppet agencies flourished.

The January 28 Incident of 1932: Japanese marines attacked the Zhabei district of Shanghai and met stiff resistance from the Chinese 19th Route Army, with heavy fighting until a March truce. It is dated by its Chinese shorthand, ‘one-two-eight.’

The Battle of Shanghai, opened on 13 August 1937 (‘eight-one-three’), the first great campaign of the full Sino-Japanese War; three months of fighting ended with the Chinese armies’ withdrawal and the start of the ‘solitary island’ years.

“Anqing Gang” (Anqing bang) is a formal name for the Green Gang, whose lore traced it to the Anqing boatmen’s guilds of the grain-transport canals. The generation-poem quoted here fixed each initiate’s seniority by the character of his rank; Huang, never formally initiated, stood outside it—hence the running joke about the ‘Tian’ generation.

A mao’er xi was an all-female Peking-opera troupe, a novelty of the day; men and women were normally kept off the stage together, so Huang’s mixed casting at the Gongwutai was a commercial innovation.

ch14.anchor: half-breed of imperialism, feudalism, and the bureaucrat-politicians
ch14.note: The narrator, Huang Zhenshi, writes as a repentant insider under the political frame of the 1980s wenshi ziliao project, and his sweeping condemnations of Huang—and of his own former life—carry that retrospective vocabulary. The eyewitness detail is valuable; the editorializing is of its moment.

Su Yu (1907–1984), one of the Communists’ ablest field commanders and the victor of the Huai-Hai campaign, was then a senior figure in the Shanghai Military Control Commission that received Huang’s written confession shortly before his death in 1953.

Wing On (Yong’an) was one of the ‘big four’ Nanjing Road department stores built by overseas-Chinese merchants; its expansion is what forced Gu Zhuxuan’s Tianchan Stage to move, touching off the lawsuit described here.
To eat ‘red-and-white rice’ was to live off the fees squeezed from weddings (red) and funerals (white)—here by forcing oneself on families as the contractor of their ceremonial processions.

To ‘drink reasoning-tea’ (chi jiangcha) was to settle a dispute by argument before an arbitrator at a teahouse, the drinks paid by the losing side—a gang custom that made teahouses like the Deyi Lou the informal courts of the underworld.

ch15.note: Fan Shaozeng (范绍增, 1894–1977), a Sichuan warlord of Paoge and Green Gang background who became Du Yuesheng's sworn brother, later commanded Nationalist troops against Japan, and went over to the Communists in December 1949. His memoir is thus an insider's, warm toward Du in its particulars and unsparing in its judgments; the political vocabulary (‘reactionaries,’ ‘counter-revolutionary’) is that of the 1980s collection in which it was published.

Shen Zui (沈醉, 1914–1996) was a senior officer of the Juntong, the Nationalist secret service under Dai Li; captured in 1949, he became, after his release, a prolific memoirist of the Nationalist intelligence world and took down or edited many of the accounts in this series. On the Juntong see the note at ch06.

The Paoge (袍哥, the ‘Gowned Brothers’) were the Sichuan branch of the Elder Brothers Society (see ch07), a sworn-brotherhood secret society that pervaded Sichuan society and its armies; a daye (‘great uncle’) was a senior lodge leader.

To become sworn brothers, two men exchanged gengtie (庚帖), cards giving each man's name and the year, month, day, and hour of his birth, binding themselves as kin of different surnames. It is a tie distinct from the master–disciple bond by which one entered a gang boss's ‘door’ (see ch03).

ch15.anchor: the Red Army under the commander He Long
ch15.note: He Long (贺龙, 1896–1969), a Communist commander who led Red Army forces in the Hunan–Hubei border fighting of the early 1930s and later became a marshal of the People's Liberation Army. Fan, then a Nationalist commander fighting against him, gives him the respectful ‘commander’ (司令员) of the account's own later standpoint.
Pao dinggong (抛顶宫), Shanghai underworld slang for snatching the hats—often costly felt or fur—off passers-by to resell them; a petty street theft.

ch15.anchor: the "Great World" amusement park that Huang Jinrong ran
ch15.note: The Great World (大世界), Shanghai's most famous amusement hall, was founded in 1917 by the entrepreneur Huang Chujiu, not by Huang Jinrong, who gained control of it only later; the narrator, like several contributors, telescopes this. Du's fruit-selling days in fact predate the hall, and other accounts place his stall elsewhere; the detail is traditional rather than documented.

ch15.anchor: the brothels of Huileli on Fourth Avenue
ch15.note: Fourth Avenue (四马路, today's Fuzhou Road) and its lane Huileli (会乐里) were the heart of Shanghai's high-class courtesan quarter. To ‘drink flower wine’ (chi huajiu) was to hold a banquet attended by singing girls.
Biesan (瘪三), a Shanghai term of contempt for a ragged street vagrant or petty beggar-thief.

Zhuge Liang (181–234), chancellor of the state of Shu Han and the proverbial master strategist of Chinese tradition; to call a man a ‘military counselor’ (junshi) or ‘a Zhuge Liang’ was to credit him with cunning resourcefulness.

Zhang Jinghu is Zhang Renkui (张仁奎), styled Jinghu, the veteran Green Gang boss and founder of the Ren Society treated at ch09; his hao appears in this collection as both Jinghu and Jinhu (锦湖). He had indeed served as garrison commander of the Tong–Hai region of northern Jiangsu.

ch15.anchor: had also entered as Zhang's disciple
ch15.note: The claim that Chiang Kai-shek took Green Gang initiation as a young man in Shanghai is often repeated in accounts like this one but is not established; it flattered the tellers, who gained face by it, and served the Communist case against Chiang. Treat it as gang lore, not fact.

Song Jiang, chief of the outlaw band of Liangshan Marsh in the novel Water Margin, was nicknamed ‘Timely Rain’ (及时雨) for his open-handed generosity to men in need—the model of the chivalrous fixer Du wished to project.
Lord Chunshen and Lord Mengchang were Warring States grandees famous for maintaining thousands of retainers; to hail Du as their latter-day equal flattered him as a great patron and host.

ch15.anchor: the Chou'an Society for Yuan Shikai
ch15.note: The Chou'an Society (筹安会) was the body that in 1915 promoted Yuan Shikai's attempt to make himself emperor; its promoters were mocked as the ‘Six Gentlemen,’ Yang Du foremost among them. On Yang Du's later career see the note at ch04.

The ‘Four Great Families’ (四大家族)—Chiang, Soong, Kung, and Chen—was the standard Communist shorthand for the clans held to have monopolized Nationalist political and financial power: Chiang Kai-shek, T. V. Soong, H. H. Kung, and the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu.

ch15.anchor: Before four o'clock on the morning of April 12
ch15.note: This is the fullest first-hand account in the collection of the coup of 12 April 1927 (see the note at ch02). It is told largely as Du himself told it to the narrator, and credits Du with the planning, the forged armbands, and the ‘collusion with the enemy’ pretext for the killings that followed. As gang men recalling their own decisive service, both teller and subject had reason to magnify Du's part.

In the French tramway, light, and power strike of 1930, French Concession police fired on strikers meeting at the union club on 21 July, killing and wounding a number of workers; the ‘July 21 tragedy’ became a landmark of the Shanghai labor movement. Du, posing as mediator, in fact worked to break the strike for the French and the Nationalists.

ch15.anchor: comprador of the French water-and-electricity company
ch15.note: A comprador (买办) was the Chinese manager who handled a foreign firm's dealings with the local market—a position of wealth and brokerage between the concession powers and Chinese society.

ch15.anchor: set Vietnamese police to open fire
ch15.note: The French Concession recruited Vietnamese (‘Annamite’) constables from its Indochina colony for its police, alongside Chinese and Sikh officers; they were widely resented as instruments of colonial control.

ch15.anchor: the White Russians whom the French imperialists
ch15.note: White Russians—émigrés who had fled the Bolshevik revolution—formed a large and often destitute stateless community in Shanghai; the concession authorities and the gangs used them as police, guards, and, as here, strikebreakers.

ch15.anchor: the Nationalist Central Committee member Li Shizeng
ch15.note: Li Shizeng (李石曾, 1881–1973), a France-educated Nationalist elder and Guomindang Central Committee member with close French ties, prominent in the anarchist and work-study movements; here he lends his standing to breaking the strike.

ch15.anchor: the Nationalists' election of a vice-president
ch15.note: At the 1948 National Assembly (the narrator dates it from 1947, when the campaign began), Chiang Kai-shek backed Sun Ke for vice-president, but Li Zongren, leader of the Guangxi faction, won—a rare open defeat for Chiang, to which Fan's vote-brokering here belongs.
‘Aviation to save the nation’ (航空救国) was a government campaign of the early 1930s to build up China's air power by public subscription; donating aircraft was a conspicuous show of patriotism.

Saionji Kinmochi (1849–1940) was the last of the Japanese genrō, the elder statesmen who guided the throne. That he received Du warmly and kept up a correspondence with him is Du's own boast, repeated here; it is otherwise unattested and improbable, and belongs with Du's cultivation of a statesmanlike image.

The Lytton Commission, sent by the League of Nations under the Earl of Lytton, came to China in 1932 to investigate Japan's seizure of Manchuria; its stop in Shanghai gave Du the chance to play host to a world body.

ch15.anchor: In the sixteenth year, when the national army
ch15.note: ‘The sixteenth year’ is 1927 in the Republican calendar. The passage, from the Nationalist party organ Central Daily News, praises Du's part in the April 12 purge in the ornate classical manner of an official eulogy; its ‘hidden brigands’ and ‘the disaffected brought to peace’ are euphemisms for the massacred Communist workers.

ch15.anchor: When Chiang stepped down the first time
ch15.note: Chiang Kai-shek resigned his commands in August 1927 amid factional conflict within the Nationalists, retiring to Shanghai and Zhejiang before returning to power at the start of 1928—the first of several tactical resignations in his career.

ch15.anchor: when Dai Ji was garrison commander
ch15.note: Dai Ji (戴戟, 1895–1973), Songhu garrison commander and a commander in the 1932 defense of Shanghai—not to be confused with Dai Li (戴笠), the secret-service chief who recurs throughout these chapters.

The Sun Sun Company (新新公司) was one of the great Chinese-owned department stores on Nanjing Road, with a rooftop amusement arcade—here the scene of a struggle between gang men and secret agents over a captured drug dealer.
Wahua (挖花) was a card game; paijiu (牌九), mentioned next, a gambling game played with dominoes. Both were staples of the private high-stakes tables of the Shanghai rich.

Da fanxi (大翻戏), literally ‘the big turn-over play,’ underworld slang for a large-scale swindle. The foreign-run horse racing, greyhound racing, and jai alai (see ch08) that follow were the licensed gambling of the concessions.
The Champions' sweepstakes (香槟赛, from the English ‘champion’) were the great lotteries run on the spring and autumn race meetings of the Shanghai Race Club, drawing enormous sums.

The fabi (法币), the Nationalist government's managed paper currency issued from 1935, collapsed into hyperinflation after the war, which is why the gamblers reckoned first in silver dollars and then in American dollars.
The Tongshang Bank (通商银行, the Commercial Bank of China), founded in 1897, was the country's first modern Chinese bank and had once issued its own banknotes.

ch15.anchor: the China Merchants' Steam Navigation Company
ch15.note: The China Merchants' Steam Navigation Company (招商局), founded in 1872, was the great semi-official Chinese shipping line—a measure of how far Du's directorships reached into the commanding heights of the economy.

At the outbreak of full war in August 1937 the Nationalists scuttled merchant and naval vessels across the Yangtze at Jiangyin, below Nanjing, to block the Japanese fleet; Du's contribution of ships from the Dada line won him credit as a patriot.

ch15.anchor: In 1932 he founded the Heng Society
ch15.note: The Heng Society (恒社), Du's disciple-fraternity, was organized as a modern club to bind his following; it is the subject of ch20, and its charter and 1934 membership roll are reproduced in the appendices. Its name puns on Du's given name (see the note at ch03). Lu Jingshi's Qing Society and Zhang Kechang's Chang Society were sub-fraternities of his disciples' disciples.

To ‘take an old man’ (拜老头子) was to enter a gang boss's discipleship, acknowledging him as one's master; Chiang Kai-shek, the narrator says, could not bear his officers to owe such allegiance to anyone but himself.

ch15.anchor: his concubine Yao Yulan was a famous performer
ch15.note: Yao Yulan (姚玉兰), a noted Peking-opera actress who became Du's fourth wife. Meng Xiaodong (孟小冬, 1908–1977), mentioned below, was the most celebrated woman performer of laosheng (old-man) roles of her day and had once been the companion of Mei Lanfang; she became Du's wife in Hong Kong in 1950.

ch15.anchor: He played Huang Tianba, Zhang played Dou Erdun
ch15.note: Huang Tianba and Dou Erdun are stock heroes of the Peking-opera repertoire (from the cycle Lianhuan tao, ‘The Linked Stratagems’), a bandit-chief and a knight-errant—robust martial roles ill-suited to two amateur gang bosses, as the fiasco that follows shows.

A wanmin san (万民伞, ‘ten-thousand-citizen umbrella’) was a large ceremonial parasol, its canopy hung with strips of silk bearing subscribers’ names, traditionally presented to a departing official or a local benefactor as a public token of gratitude. That gangsters and shopkeepers heaped them on Du marks how thoroughly he had taken on the trappings of a civic worthy.

Xiao si bu kui (孝思不匡), a phrase from the Classic of Poetry (‘filial thoughts that never fail’), long a stock inscription for ancestral halls. On a plaque from Chiang Kai-shek to a Green Gang boss’s new shrine, it lends the state’s sanction to Du’s claim of ancestral piety.

The panegyrists pun twice on Du Yuesheng’s surname, 杜 (Du). Wu Peifu’s plaque had made him heir to the Jin-dynasty general Du Yu, nicknamed ‘Du of the Arsenal’; the literary men’s parallel-prose eulogy now casts him as a second Du Fu (712–770), the greatest of the Tang poets — grandiloquence resting on nothing but the shared surname.

ch15.anchor: puffed him up into a Guo Ziyi
ch15.note: Guo Ziyi (697–781), the Tang general who broke the An Lushan rebellion and lived to great age laden with honors and ringed by sons and grandsons, is the Chinese byword for a life complete in rank, wealth, longevity, and posterity. To liken a gang boss to him was flattery of the most extravagant kind.

ch15.anchor: the issue of the gold yuan certificate
ch15.note: The gold yuan (jinyuanquan, 金圆券), issued in August 1948 to replace the ruined fabi, was the Nationalists’ last currency reform. Backed by forced surrender of the people’s gold, silver, and foreign exchange and by rigid price ceilings, it collapsed within months into hyperinflation, wiping out urban savings and hastening the regime’s fall. Chiang Ching-kuo’s attempt to enforce it in Shanghai is the ‘tiger-beating’ of these pages.

ch15.anchor: the Juntong Bureau and the Sino-American Cooperation Organization
ch15.note: The Sino-American Cooperation Organization (SACO, 中美合作所), formed in 1943, was a wartime intelligence partnership between Dai Li’s Juntong and the U.S. Navy, its American side headed by Commodore Milton E. Miles (the ‘Miles’ below). It trained and armed Nationalist agents and guerrillas; its Chongqing compound was notorious for its interrogation prison.

ch15.anchor: a department head of the Baomiju
ch15.note: The Baomiju (保密局, Bureau of Confidential Affairs) was the postwar renaming, in 1946, of Dai Li’s Juntong secret service. Shen Zui — the very officer named here as sent to stop the killing — is the man who set this memoir down from Fan Shaozeng’s telling; the recorder thus steps, for a moment, into his own account.

The shangfang sword (上方宝剣), in old drama a sword of state bestowed by the emperor, empowered its bearer to put high officials to death on his own authority and report afterward. The figure casts Chiang Ching-kuo as wielding his father’s delegated power to strike without check.

The Loyal and Patriotic Army (Zhongyi Jiuguo Jun, 忠义救国军) was the guerrilla force Dai Li built from Green Gang irregulars in the Shanghai region after 1937; nominally anti-Japanese, it served as much to hold the underworld and, later, to fight the Communists.

一品老百姓 — a wry coinage. Yipin, ‘first rank,’ was the highest of the nine grades of imperial officialdom, so a ‘first-rank commoner’ is a man of the very greatest standing who yet holds no office at all: the foremost of nobodies.
